text: India has a lake inside a crater blasted out by a space rock. A canyon that looks like it belongs in Arizona. Bridges that are alive, and keep growing. And a frozen river you can walk on for days. Most Indians have never seen any of them. Today, let's look at India at its true scale.
This is True Scale. First, a quick sense of just how big some of India's states really are.

Rajasthan, India's largest state, covers about three hundred and forty-two thousand square kilometres. Let's lift it up and drop it onto Europe. It's bigger than Italy. It's bigger than Poland. Now look at Goa, India's smallest state, at about three thousand seven hundred square kilometres. You could fit Goa inside Rajasthan more than ninety times. Same country, completely different scales.

Let's start the journey in Karnataka. About sixty kilometres west of Bengaluru rises Savandurga, often described as one of the largest monolith hills in Asia. A monolith is a single, massive piece of rock. Savandurga's twin peaks climb to about twelve hundred metres above sea level, and the climb up its bare granite slopes is one of the most popular day hikes near the city. A single stone, the size of a hill.

Now head north, to Maharashtra. In the middle of farmland sits Lonar Lake, inside a crater almost two kilometres wide and about a hundred and fifty metres deep. It was created when a meteorite slammed into the Earth. Scientists still debate exactly when, with estimates from around fifty thousand years ago to over half a million. The water is salty and strongly alkaline. And in June twenty twenty, almost overnight, the whole lake turned pink, thanks to salt-loving microbes.

Next, Andhra Pradesh. At Gandikota, the Penna River has carved a deep, narrow gorge through red rock, earning it the nickname, the Grand Canyon of India. Right on the edge of the cliffs stands a fort with a history going back around eight hundred years. You can camp on the rim and watch the sunrise light up the canyon walls, often with hardly anyone else around.

Further west, in Gujarat, lies the Great Rann of Kutch, a vast white salt desert that floods in the monsoon and dries into a cracked, glittering plain. And on an island in the middle of it sits Dholavira, a city built by the Indus Valley Civilisation, more than four thousand years ago. Its people built a system of reservoirs to catch every drop of rain. In twenty twenty-one, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Now to Assam, and the mighty Brahmaputra. In the middle of the river sits Majuli, recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's largest river island. It's home to more than one hundred and sixty thousand people and centuries-old Vaishnavite monasteries called satras. But the river is slowly eating it. In the seventeen nineties, Majuli covered about thirteen hundred square kilometres. Today, it's closer to nine hundred. Visit it while you can.

Next door, in Meghalaya, the Khasi and Jaintia people grow their bridges. They guide the roots of rubber fig trees across rivers, and over years, the roots thicken into bridges strong enough to walk on. There are about a hundred of them, spread across nearly seventy villages, and some are even double-deckers. They need the rain, and Meghalaya has plenty. The village of Mawsynram averages almost twelve thousand millimetres of rain a year, one of the highest totals on Earth.

And in Arunachal Pradesh, there's Ziro Valley, home of the Apatani people. They farm rice and fish together in the same flooded fields, a system so efficient it's on UNESCO's tentative list for World Heritage. Pine-covered hills, bamboo, and almost no crowds. If you want somewhere that feels truly different, this is it.

And one more for the list. High in Uttarakhand, the Valley of Flowers explodes into colour every monsoon, with hundreds of species of wildflowers carpeting the slopes. Together with the neighbouring Nanda Devi National Park, it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site. And yet, it's open for only a few months a year, and you can only reach it on foot.

Now, let's talk treks, and compare a few of India's most famous ones side by side. Kedarkantha in Uttarakhand tops out at about three thousand eight hundred metres, and it's a favourite first snow trek for beginners. Sandakphu, in West Bengal, is a little lower, at about three thousand six hundred metres. The Chadar trek in Ladakh stays at around three thousand four hundred metres, but in deep winter. Hampta Pass in Himachal climbs to over four thousand two hundred metres. And Roopkund reaches about five thousand metres.

So why choose one over another? Sandakphu is the highest point in West Bengal, and from its summit you can see four of the five highest mountains on Earth: Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse and Makalu. All in one sunrise. That's a view most climbers would pay a fortune for, and it's reachable on a moderate trek.

Roopkund is the mystery. It's a small glacial lake, high in the Himalayas, known as Skeleton Lake. The remains of more than three hundred people have been found around it. A twenty nineteen study found that they didn't all die together. Some died around the ninth century. Others, with ancestry linked to the eastern Mediterranean, died around eighteen hundred. Nobody knows exactly why.

And Chadar is the wildest of them all. In January and February, the Zanskar River in Ladakh freezes over, and for generations, it was the only winter route in and out of the valley. Trekkers walk along the frozen river, in temperatures that can drop to minus thirty degrees. In some recent winters, the ice hasn't formed properly, and the trek has had to stop.

A meteorite crater, a living bridge, a disappearing island, a lake of skeletons. India is far bigger, and far stranger, than most of us realise. Which one would you visit first? Tell me in the comments. And if you enjoyed this, subscribe to True Scale for more.
